Trying to Conceive

Preparing a semen sample: collection, transport and questions before the test

Updated: November 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A semen analysis examines more than sperm count. How the sample is collected and delivered helps the laboratory interpret its findings. Start with the instructions from the laboratory that will receive it, because appointment, container, abstinence and transport requirements differ. Needing help to provide a sample is a practical concern the team can discuss without judging you.

Understand why the test is part of assessment

Fertility difficulties can involve either partner, both partners or factors that remain unexplained after assessment. A known condition in one partner does not establish that the other partner’s fertility is normal. Semen testing can contribute to a coordinated evaluation and treatment plan; it is not a test of masculinity, sexual performance or personal worth.

Tell the clinician why the test was requested. A diagnostic fertility assessment, a sample for treatment and a post-vasectomy check can have different instructions and interpretations. This guide concerns diagnostic collection. Do not use a general article or a home sperm-count result to decide whether contraception can be stopped after a vasectomy.

Arrange the appointment and collection location first

Contact the receiving laboratory before collecting anything. Confirm the referral, appointment, identification documents, approved container and how the sample will be handed over. Ask whether there is a private collection room at your chosen site. Different branches of the same service may have different facilities; do not assume that an unbooked sample can be accepted.

If you prefer home collection, ask whether it is allowed and whether your journey meets the laboratory’s delivery window. Discuss privacy, accessibility, language support and any assistance you need in advance. Obtain the written instructions and a contact number so that a delay or collection problem can be resolved before you travel.

Count abstinence from ejaculation

For a standard diagnostic sample, the WHO manual commonly uses two to seven days without ejaculation. This includes ejaculation during masturbation as well as intercourse. Your laboratory may request a narrower interval, so follow its exact instruction and record how long you actually abstained. More days is not automatically a better way to prepare.

If you ejaculated within the requested interval, had an involuntary ejaculation or cannot meet the timing, tell the laboratory and ask whether to keep the appointment. Do not give an inaccurate date to make the sample seem acceptable. Treatment-related collections may have different requirements; instructions for one test should not be transferred automatically to another.

Report fever, illness and substantial heat exposure

A recent fever or illness can temporarily affect semen findings. Tell the team when it happened, how unwell you were and whether you are still recovering. The clinician may decide to test now, repeat later or change the appointment according to the clinical question. Do not assume that every illness requires the same waiting period or that an abnormal result after fever proves a permanent problem.

Also mention repeated hot-tub or sauna use and significant occupational heat exposure. Sensible longer-term health changes are different from trying to alter a result in a few days. Ask whether your circumstances require a change in exposure or test timing. Discuss smoking, alcohol, caffeine intake and recreational drugs honestly; a one-week detox cannot guarantee a normal sample.

Bring a complete medicine and supplement list

Include prescription medicines, non-prescription products, vitamins, herbal or bodybuilding supplements, doses, routes and recent changes. Mention medicines used for hair loss, urinary symptoms, blood pressure, inflammation, infection or cancer, as well as testosterone. An effect on ejaculation, sexual function or a semen measurement does not necessarily show an effect on the chance of pregnancy.

Do not stop, skip or switch prescribed treatment to improve the test. The prescriber may want a sample while treatment continues, may review a possible contribution or may arrange follow-up after a supervised change. The underlying illness can also affect the findings. A laboratory result and a medicine name alone cannot establish the cause.

Hair-loss and prostate medicines are not one uniform group

Finasteride and dutasteride are 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors. Their product information describes different semen findings and reports, with uncertainty about what they mean for individual fertility. Dose, indication and the person studied matter. Information from a 5 mg finasteride study should not be treated as proof that everyone taking a different dose will become infertile.

Alpha blockers such as silodosin, tamsulosin and alfuzosin also differ. Some can reduce or alter ejaculation, and a dry or smaller ejaculate is not the same as proven failure to produce sperm. Short studies of semen measurements cannot establish a class-wide effect on conception. Report the exact product and symptoms rather than changing treatment yourself.

Other named medicines need specific interpretation

Sulfasalazine has been associated with low sperm counts and male infertility that may improve after withdrawal, but the disease still needs treatment and recovery is not guaranteed on a fixed schedule. Colchicine has rare reports of potentially reversible fertility problems; the illness it treats can itself be relevant. Oral ketoconazole can affect testosterone and sperm-related measures. That does not establish the same risk for a topical cream or shampoo.

Spironolactone’s antiandrogenic and sexual effects warrant an individual review. Nifedipine information describes limited reports involving sperm function in IVF, not proof that it lowers everyone’s sperm count. Cimetidine’s product label reports no effect in human studies on sperm production, count, movement or shape; taking it does not establish that it caused an abnormal semen result. Sexual side effects are a separate question.

Distinguish infection treatment, steroids and cancer care

Antibiotics are not a single category that can be said to lower sperm count. The infection, associated fever, exact drug and clinical situation all matter. Prescribed corticosteroids also differ from anabolic steroids used for bodybuilding; the evidence does not support treating every steroid preparation as equivalent. In particular, do not abruptly stop prescribed corticosteroids. Exogenous testosterone can suppress sperm production and is not a fertility booster; discuss conception plans with its prescriber.

Cancer and cancer-directed treatment may affect fertility in different ways. If treatment is planned, ask the oncology team promptly about fertility preservation, ideally before treatment begins. Some people may need specialist help if they cannot provide an ejaculated sample. Do not delay or stop cancer treatment on your own, assume every regimen causes permanent infertility, or rely on a universal recovery interval.

Use the supplied container and collect the whole sample

Use the container supplied or specifically approved by the laboratory. Follow the laboratory’s instructions for washing your hands and penis, rinsing away soap and drying as directed. Avoid touching the inside of the pot or lid. The usual method is masturbation directly into the container, collecting the whole ejaculate rather than trying to produce a particular volume. The pot does not need to be filled.

Close the lid securely and complete the required identifiers, collection time and other paperwork. Tell the laboratory if any portion was missed, especially the first portion. Do not scoop spilled semen back into the pot, add water or another substance, or hide a problem. The team can decide whether the sample is interpretable or should be repeated.

Ask before using lubricant or a collection condom

Do not use saliva, an ordinary lubricant or a consumer condom unless the laboratory has specifically approved it for this collection. Materials and additives can interfere with the sample. A product described as non-spermicidal or fertility-friendly is not automatically validated for diagnostic testing. If lubrication is needed, ask for an approved option before the appointment.

When masturbation is not suitable, some laboratories can arrange a specially approved collection condom for intercourse. This needs discussion and specific handling instructions; sample loss and contamination remain possible. Do not improvise with withdrawal or an ordinary condom. Ask whether transfer to the laboratory container is required and exactly how to deliver the sample.

Protect the sample during transport

For approved home collection, establish the maximum time to delivery and the temperature instructions before starting. Semen examination is time-sensitive. A statement that delivery should take at least two hours is wrong; waiting that long may make a sample unsuitable. Different laboratories specify different shorter windows, so use the receiving service’s instructions rather than choosing the longest allowance found online.

Record the collection time, secure the container in the supplied packaging and avoid overheating or chilling it. Do not refrigerate, freeze, place on a radiator or use a heating pad unless the laboratory has given a specific instruction for a different type of test. If traffic, a spill or another delay disrupts the plan, call the laboratory and report what happened instead of guessing whether the sample is still usable.

If anxiety or difficulty producing the sample gets in the way

An unfamiliar room, time pressure, pain, disability, personal beliefs or worries about results can make collection difficult. Tell the team which part is a problem. Depending on the service and clinical circumstances, they may discuss another appointment, a more suitable setting, approved home collection or an alternative collection method. These options must be arranged, rather than assumed to be available everywhere.

You do not need to conceal a failed attempt or force yourself to continue in distress. Ask how to contact staff privately and how your information and results will be handled. A sample problem does not define your fertility or your relationship. If reluctance is delaying assessment, discuss the concern with the clinician so that support and an acceptable plan can be considered.

Know what is being measured

Semen includes sperm made in the testes and fluid from glands, particularly the seminal vesicles and prostate. The amount of fluid is not the same as the number of sperm. A visible ejaculate can contain few or no sperm, and appearance cannot establish fertility. A fixed percentage of semen described as sperm is not a useful personal test.

The report may assess volume, concentration, total sperm number, movement, shape and other features. Its reference values describe measurements in a particular context; they are not a simple fertile-versus-infertile boundary. Ask the clinician to interpret the full pattern with the collection details and both partners’ history. Home kits may measure only part of what a laboratory analysis assesses.

Agree when a repeat sample is useful

There is no universal rule that everyone needs two samples exactly one month apart. A repeat may clarify an abnormal finding, assess a collection problem or help answer a treatment question. NICE’s current fertility guidance recommends confirming an abnormal initial result, ideally around three months later, but repeating as soon as possible when no sperm or a severe reduction is found.

WHO’s 2025 infertility guideline suggests a repeat after at least eleven weeks when one or more parameters are outside its reference ranges, with very low certainty of evidence; it does not suggest routine repetition when all are within range in that assessment context. These recommendations need clinical interpretation. Ask why your interval was chosen, and do not postpone assessment of a severe result simply to meet a general waiting rule.

Keep symptoms separate from the routine test appointment

A semen test does not replace assessment of a new lump, swelling or worrying testicular discomfort. Arrange urgent clinical advice for these changes rather than waiting for a laboratory result. Mention pain, ejaculation changes, medicines and recent illness to the clinician; the next investigation should address the actual concern.

Seek emergency care for sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or testicular pain lasting more than an hour or continuing at rest. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask another person to take you or call for an ambulance. Do not delay urgent help to finish an abstinence interval or produce a sample.

Leave with a clear follow-up plan

Before leaving, confirm that the laboratory has the collection details and knows about any lost sample, delay, fever or medicine change. Ask when results are expected, who will explain them and how to follow up if they do not arrive. Keep the test instructions and the actual collection details together so that a repeat can be compared fairly.

The aim is a reliable assessment that helps guide care, not a perfect-looking result. An abnormal finding does not automatically mean that pregnancy is impossible, and a reassuring report does not explain every fertility difficulty. Follow the agreed review plan and discuss any treatment decision with the responsible clinician.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Obtain the receiving laboratory’s written instructions, confirm the appointment and prepare the approved container and delivery plan.

Record the actual abstinence interval and collection time; tell the team about fever, medicines, loss of sample, difficulty or delay.

Arrange a result review and an individualized repeat plan; ask for practical collection support and seek symptom-based urgent care when needed.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you keep appointment details, medicine lists and questions in one place. It cannot approve a collection method, judge whether a delayed sample is usable, interpret fertility from a report or replace laboratory instructions and clinical assessment. Contact the team directly when the plan changes.

When to seek help

Do not stop prescribed medicines to improve a semen result or improvise collection supplies. Seek urgent advice for a new testicular lump, swelling or worrying discomfort. Sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting more than an hour or continuing at rest needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself; arrange another driver or an ambulance. Do not delay urgent assessment for a sample appointment.

Evidence notes updated: November 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Arrange the appointment, approved container, collection location and delivery plan before producing a sample.
  • Follow the laboratory’s abstinence interval, counted from ejaculation, and report what actually happened.
  • Disclose recent fever, medicines and collection problems; do not stop prescribed treatment to change a result.
  • Use only laboratory-approved collection materials and tell staff about sample loss or transport delays.
  • Agree how results and any repeat test will be interpreted, and seek urgent help for concerning symptoms independently of the test.

Frequently asked questions

Can a fever affect a semen test?

Yes, recent fever or illness can temporarily affect findings. Tell the team when it occurred and whether you have recovered. The clinician can decide whether to test now or change the timing; there is no single waiting period for every illness.

Can I use lubricant or saliva to collect the sample?

Avoid saliva and unapproved lubricants. Ask the receiving laboratory for a validated option if needed. A consumer product labelled fertility-friendly is not automatically suitable for diagnostic collection.

How far apart should two semen tests be?

The interval depends on the result and purpose. NICE advises confirmation of an abnormal result ideally around three months later, but as soon as possible for absent or severely reduced sperm. WHO’s conditional eleven-week suggestion has a defined context and very low-certainty evidence. Do not assume everyone must wait the same interval.

How long should I avoid ejaculation before the test?

Two to seven days is a common diagnostic standard, but laboratories may specify a narrower window. Count ejaculation during masturbation as well as intercourse, follow your service’s instructions and report the actual interval.

Can I collect at home or during intercourse?

Sometimes, after arranging it with the laboratory. Home collection must meet its transport requirements. Intercourse collection requires a specially approved method and supplies; do not use an ordinary condom or withdrawal as a substitute.

What if I spill part of the sample or cannot produce one?

Tell the laboratory, including whether the first portion was lost. Do not put spilled material back into the container. If collection is difficult, ask for support or another arrangement; a failed attempt is not a fertility diagnosis.

Should I stop medicines before testing?

No, not on your own. Bring a complete list and discuss the exact product, dose, route and symptoms. Medicines can affect different endpoints, and the illness itself may matter. The clinician may want to assess the sample while treatment continues or plan a supervised review.

Does an abnormal result mean pregnancy is impossible?

No. The whole report, collection quality and both partners’ circumstances need interpretation. Some people conceive naturally despite an abnormal measurement; others need further assessment or treatment. New lumps or swelling need urgent advice, and emergency testicular-pain symptoms should not wait for test results.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
